s: A whole village of transplanted wooden churches
w: An open-air skansen where entire wooden churches, farmhouses and windmills - carried here piece by piece from villages across western Ukraine - stand together under one roof of trees. Named for the Klymentiy Sheptytsky Museum of Folk Architecture it houses, it's rural Galicia condensed into a single walkable park.
_facts: Open-air museum (skansen) of folk architecture and rural life in Lviv
Also known as the Klymentiy Sheptytsky Museum of Folk Architecture and Rural Life
Also known by the name Shevchenkivskyi Hai

s: Traditionally the oldest church still standing in Lviv
w: Tucked beneath Budelnytsia Hora on what was once the Volynskyi Trakt, this Orthodox church is widely held to be the oldest in the city, though its exact founding has faded into tradition rather than record. Still an active parish, and a protected architectural monument of national importance.
_facts: Religious building in Lviv, active temple of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine
Architectural monument of national importance, traditionally the oldest church in the city
Located under Budelnytsia Hora at 28 Bohdan Khmelnytskyi Street, formerly Volynskyi Trakt

s: A Neo-classical column for Poland's greatest Romantic poet
w: Raised in 1904 at what's now Mickiewicz Square, this column honours Adam Mickiewicz, the Polish Romantic poet whose verse the city claimed as its own even though he never lived there. It's one of many Mickiewicz monuments scattered across the old Polish-Lithuanian lands - civic memory built into recurring architecture.
_facts: Neo-classical column commemorating Polish Romantic poet Adam Mickiewicz (1798-1855)
Located at Mickiewicz Square in the centre of Lviv
Opened in 1904

s: A Renaissance mansion blackened dark by centuries of weather
w: Built in 1577 for the Italian tax collector Tomaso Alberti, its sandstone facade has darkened to a near-black over four and a half centuries, giving the building its name. A later owner added a storey and opened one of the city's first pharmacies downstairs; today it houses the Lviv Historical Museum.
_facts: Renaissance building on Market Square in Lviv, built for Tomaso Alberti in 1577
Facade lined with sandstone that has darkened over the years to blackish brown
Jan Lorencowicz added a storey and opened one of the town's first pharmacies in 1596; Lviv Historical Museum housed here since 1926

s: Where Ukraine's independence was proclaimed under occupation
w: Prince Stanisław Lubomirski built this Market Square palace in the 1760s, and for half a century after 1771 it housed Austria's governors of Galicia. Bought by Ukrainian society Prosvita in the 19th century, it turned into a nationalist hub - and in 1941, Stetsko proclaimed independence from inside its walls.
_facts: Palace of Prince Stanislaw Lubomirski, built 1760s to Jan de Witte's design, main facade on Market Square
Served as residence of Austrian governors of Galicia 1771-1821; purchased by Ukrainian organization Prosvita in the 19th century
Yaroslav Stetsko proclaimed Ukraine's independence here days after the Nazi invasion of the Soviet Union

s: Ukraine's oldest synagogue, destroyed by the Nazis in 1941
w: Established in 1582, the Golden Rose was the oldest synagogue on the territory of modern Ukraine and, from 1603, the main communal synagogue of Lviv's Jewish community. Nazi Germany destroyed it in the Second World War, along with the neighbouring Great City Synagogue - its ruins kept today as a memorial.
_facts: Orthodox Jewish synagogue established 1582, oldest synagogue on the territory of modern Ukraine
Served as main communal synagogue of Lviv from 1603 to 1801
Destroyed by the Nazis during World War II, along with the Great City Synagogue

s: A railway baron's mansion, later a Soviet school
w: This Chateauesque mansion from the 1870s belonged to Prince Adam Sapieha, a pioneer of Galician railway building, screened from the road by a wrought-iron grille. Soviet forces seized it after the 1939 invasion of Poland and ran a school out of it for decades before a restoration handed it to a heritage society.
_facts: Chateauesque two-storey mansion in Lviv dating from the 1870s
First owner Prince Adam Sapieha, a pioneer of railway building in Galicia
Housed a school after the Soviet invasion of 1939; restored in the 1990s, now home to a regional heritage preservation society

s: The mother church of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic faith
w: Built between 1744 and 1760 on a hill above the city, this baroque-rococo cathedral is the third church on a site fought over since the 1200s - repeatedly targeted by invaders and vandals for exactly why it mattered so much: for two centuries it served as mother church of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church.
_facts: Baroque-rococo cathedral in Lviv, constructed 1744-1760 on a hill overlooking the city
Third church to occupy the site since the 13th century
Served as the mother church of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church during the 19th and 20th centuries

n: Lviv Theatre of Opera and Ballet
s: Built on drained marshland, once faced a Lenin statue
w: Raised between 1897 and 1900 over the buried Poltva River, this opera house has worn several names across several regimes - the Grand Theatre under Poland, then, for four decades, the Ivan Franko, after the city's own poet. Soviet-era patrons walked in past a towering Lenin statue; the Lviv Opera outlasted him easily.
_facts: Opera house in Lviv designed by Zygmunt Gorgolewski, built 1897-1900 over the buried Poltva River
Known as the Grand Theatre under the Second Polish Republic, and the Ivan Franko Theatre for four decades under Soviet rule
Patrons under Soviet rule passed a statue of Vladimir Lenin on entering

s: The 'Wallachian Church,' still Orthodox after everything
w: Historically known as the Wallachian Church, this Orthodox building in Lviv's old town has kept both its name and its congregation through Polish, Austrian and Soviet rule alike. It now belongs to the Lviv Diocese of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine, a quiet survivor among the city's UNESCO-listed skyline of spires.
_facts: Ukrainian Orthodox church in Lviv, historically known as the Wallachian Church
Also called the Dormition or Assumption Church
Belongs to the Lviv Diocese of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine

s: A 14th-century square, four fountains, forty-four facades
w: Laid out when King Casimir the Great founded the new Lviv in the mid-1300s, Rynok Square runs 142 by 129 metres and is ringed by 44 tenement houses spanning Renaissance to Modernist styles. Four corner fountains from 1793 depict Neptune, Diana, Amphitrite and Adonis; a pillory once stood in front of the town hall.
_facts: Central square of Lviv, laid out as the central square of the new city founded by King Casimir III the Great in the mid-14th century
142 by 129 metres, ringed by 44 tenement houses in styles from Renaissance to Modernism
Four corner fountains from 1793 depicting Neptune, Diana, Amphitrite and Adonis; recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998

s: A former Galician parliament, remade into a stage
w: Built in the mid-nineteenth century to house the Galician Diet, this building on Prospekt Svobody spent the years to the First World War doubling as a theatre before drama took over for good. It's named for Maria Zankovetska, a founding figure of Ukrainian professional theatre, and still stages her legacy today.
_facts: Drama theatre in the centre of Lviv, at the intersection of Lesya Ukrayinka Street and Prospekt Svobody
Building erected mid-19th century, originally home of the Galician parliament (Diet)
Used as a theatre stage throughout the period until World War I; named for actress Maria Zankovetska

s: A Baroque church the Soviets turned into a book warehouse
w: The Jesuits raised this Baroque church between 1610 and 1630; the Soviet government closed it in 1946 and spent decades using it to store books instead of holding services. Restored and handed to the Ukrainian Greek-Catholic Church in 2010, it was reconsecrated in 2011 and now serves as a garrison church.
_facts: Historic Baroque church in Lviv built by the Society of Jesus 1610-1630, also known as Saints Peter and Paul Garrison Church
Closed by the Soviet government in 1946, used as a warehouse and book depository for decades
Turned over to the Ukrainian Greek-Catholic Church in 2010, reconsecrated in 2011; now a garrison church

n: Borys Voznytskyi Lviv National Art Gallery
s: Ukraine's largest art museum; its director was executed
w: Founded 1907 and spread across the historic Łoziński and Potocki Palaces, this collection of 62,000-plus works survived Soviet suspicion of nationally-minded museums and the chaos of World War II - during which its wartime director, Ivan Ivanets, was kidnapped by SMERSH and executed. Now Ukraine's largest art museum.
_facts: Largest art museum in Ukraine, with over 62,000 artworks
Municipal gallery decision made 1897, formally opened as Lviv Art Gallery in 1907; housed in the Łoziński and Potocki Palaces
Wartime director Ivan Ivanets kidnapped by Soviet SMERSH and executed in 1946

n: Church of St. Olha and Elizabeth
s: A neo-Gothic spire built to greet arrivals off the train
w: Architect Teodor Talowski designed this Catholic church, twin-towered with an 85-metre belfry, as the first landmark travellers saw arriving by rail - a Ukrainian answer to Vienna's Votive Church. Bomb-damaged in 1939 and left to rot as a Soviet warehouse, it was reconsecrated as a Greek Catholic parish in 1991.
_facts: Catholic church in Lviv between the main rail station and the Old Town, built 1903-1911, designed by Teodor Talowski in neo-Gothic style
Twin-towered facade with an 85m belfry, envisioned as the city's first landmark greeting rail arrivals
Damaged by bombing in 1939, used as a warehouse after the war; reconsecrated as a Ukrainian Greek Catholic parish in 1991

s: The Greek Catholic archbishops' seat since the 1500s
w: Rebuilt in 1761-62 to Clement Fessinger's designs opposite St. George's Cathedral, this palace has housed the Metropolitans of the Ukrainian Greek-Catholic Church since the 16th century, its style shifting from Baroque toward Neo-Classical. Pope John Paul II stayed here during his 2001 visit to Ukraine.
_facts: Principal residence of the Metropolitans of the Ukrainian Greek-Catholic Church since the 16th century
Current building erected 1761-62 to Clement Fessinger's designs, opposite St. George's Cathedral
Pope John Paul II stayed at the palace during his 2001 visit to Ukraine

s: A Polish library nationalised wholesale by the Soviets
w: Founded in 1940 from the collections of the Ossolineum and other major libraries, nationalised en masse after the Soviet invasion of Poland, this is now one of Ukraine's great research archives. Archaeologist Larysa Krushelnytska, appointed to lead it in 1991, pushed its post-independence development furthest.
_facts: National Scientific Library of Ukraine in Lviv, established 2 January 1940
Headquarters in the Ossolineum building; holdings nationalized after the Soviet invasion of Poland
Named after Vasyl Stefanyk in 1971; Larysa Krushelnytska appointed head in October 1991

s: A Hasidic synagogue, now a Jewish history museum
w: Also called the Chasidim Synagogue, this building on Vuhilna Street served as an active Orthodox Hasidic synagogue from 1844 to 1962, weathering repurposing through World War II and Soviet occupation. Since 1995 it has operated as a Jewish history museum and cultural centre, preserving what the war years nearly erased.
_facts: Former Orthodox Hasidic Jewish synagogue at Vuhilna Street No. 3 in Lviv, also called the Chasidim Synagogue
Operated as a synagogue from 1844 until 1962
Preserved as a Jewish history museum and cultural center since 1995
